scenarios.title: Help when the puck changes teams
scenarios.objective: Recognize a change from attacking to defending and choose a helpful route back.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. Gold1 has just taken the puck near the middle. YOU are above the play and Navy2 is between YOU and the navy end. The coach says the team roles changed when Gold1 got the puck.
cues: Navy2 is closer to the navy end.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck now?

options.text: Gold1
YOU
Navy2

questions.explanation: Gold1 is the puck owner in this freeze. That means navy players need to think about helping defend.

questions.prompt: What should YOU notice after the change?

options.text: Gold1 has the puck
Navy2 is nearer the navy end
Navy2 is between YOU and Gold1

questions.explanation: The new puck owner and the teammate nearer the navy end are what this freeze actually shows. Navy2 stands farther back toward the navy end, not between YOU and Gold1, so YOU are the navy player still high in the attacking end.

questions.prompt: Place YOU between Gold1 and the navy end to help.
questions.explanation: This example brings YOU back toward the play and the navy end while keeping Gold1 in view. The best route depends on the moving players.

questions.prompt: Arrange the role-change read.

options.text: Notice Gold1 has it
Turn toward the navy end
Skate back while watching the play

questions.explanation: Recognize the new owner, turn toward the end you protect, and skate back while keeping the puck picture. The order teaches awareness before effort.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 shifts across the lane. What should guide YOU?

options.text: Keep the puck carrier and Navy2 in view
Chase Gold1 without looking for Navy2
Stop watching because Navy2 is closer

questions.explanation: The freeze does not show Gold1 moving, so this is an imagined change. Where the puck carrier goes changes your route. Seeing both the puck carrier and Navy2 helps YOU pick a useful support route instead of guessing.

questions.prompt: Why did your job change when Gold1 got the puck?
questions.explanation: Navy no longer controls the puck, so helping protect the navy end matters first. Turning back and watching Gold1 lets YOU choose a useful support route.

scenarios.title: Turn your body to the safe side
scenarios.objective: Use body position and a changing pressure cue to protect a loose carry.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. YOU have the puck beside the boards. Gold1 is on your inside side. Navy2 is farther ahead on the wall side. The coach asks you to keep the puck away from Gold1 and look for Navy2.
cues: YOU have the puck by the boards.
Navy2 is ahead on the wall side.

questions.prompt: Which player is closer to the middle of the ice than YOU?

options.text: Gold1
Navy2
Nobody

questions.explanation: Gold1 is nearer the middle. Navy2 is closer to the side boards. Check Gold1 before moving toward the middle.

questions.prompt: What can help protect the puck?

options.text: Keep your body between Gold1 and the puck
Look for Navy2 ahead
Send the puck up the wall without looking

questions.explanation: Keeping your body between Gold1 and the puck can help protect it. Looking for Navy2 helps YOU decide whether a pass is available. Sending the puck along the wall without checking can give Gold1 a chance to reach it.

questions.prompt: Place YOU a little closer to the wall side, away from Gold1.
questions.explanation: This example gives YOU more wall-side space from Gold1 and keeps Navy2 in the forward picture. Another controlled spot can work.

questions.prompt: Put the protection read in order.

options.text: Notice Gold1 inside
Keep the puck on the far side
Look for Navy2 or new room

questions.explanation: The defender's side tells you where the first pressure is. Protect there, then scan for a teammate or a better lane.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 reaches the wall side too. What is a smart update?

options.text: Look for another lane before carrying on
Keep the puck there without looking
Send the pass to Navy2 without checking the lane

questions.explanation: Imagine Gold1 moving toward the wall side. Check how much room and reach Gold1 has now. A turn, a clear pass to Navy2 or protecting the puck may help; the next choice depends on what is still open.

questions.prompt: Why keep the puck away from Gold1?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is inside YOU, so the puck is easier to reach there. Keeping your body between the defender and puck can buy a moment to see Navy2 or another lane.

scenarios.title: Look beyond the nearest jersey
scenarios.objective: Compare a nearby covered teammate with another support option.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have the puck. Navy2 is nearby, but Gold1 occupies the direct line to Navy2. Navy3 is farther away at another angle; Gold2 is away from that illustrated line. Compare the options before trying a pass. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Gold1 sits on that near line.

questions.prompt: Which teammate is nearer YOU?

options.text: Navy3
Navy2
They are equally far

questions.explanation: Navy2 is the nearby partner on the same line.

questions.prompt: Where is Gold1 standing in this picture?

options.text: Close to YOU, almost on the line to Navy2
Beside Navy3, far up the ice
Far behind YOU, near the navy end

questions.explanation: Gold1 is two and a half metres from YOU, closer still to the puck, and almost exactly on the line from the puck to Navy2. Gold1 is more than eleven metres from Navy3, and stands ahead of YOU rather than behind.

questions.prompt: What should you compare besides distance?

options.text: Defender locations
Available passing angles
Whether a teammate is always closest

questions.explanation: Distance alone does not establish availability.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little to inspect a different passing angle.
questions.explanation: This changes the relationship to both targets. It is exploratory; the final choice still depends on defenders and puck travel.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold2 closes Navy3's line before you pass. What could you do?

options.text: Recheck both options before passing
Pass to Navy3 anyway because that was the plan
Watch Gold1 only and stop tracking Gold2

questions.explanation: The suggested preference changes when a line closes. Passing on the old plan sends the puck toward the new pressure, and tracking one defender only hides the change. If Gold2 stops short and the line stays open, Navy3 can still be a good choice.

questions.prompt: Why might the farther teammate be worth a look here?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is close but Gold1 sits on that line. Navy3 is at a different angle, though Gold1 is also near the start of that longer line in this picture, so neither pass is simply open. A useful answer says the far option is worth checking and that moving the puck first can change both angles.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 moves off the line to Navy2 and comes at YOU from the side. What can change?

options.text: The line to Navy2 can open up
Navy2 becomes a worse option every time
Nothing changes until YOU pass

questions.explanation: Moving off that line may leave Navy2 available, while Gold1 coming closer gives YOU less time. Check Gold1's reach and the lane before passing; movement alone does not guarantee an opening.

questions.prompt: Which two checks help YOU judge a pass to Navy3?

options.text: Whether Navy3 is ready to receive
Whether Gold1 or Gold2 can reach the passing lane
Whether Navy2 is the closest teammate

questions.explanation: Check the receiver and the whole passing lane. Gold1 is close to the puck and Gold2 is nearer Navy3. Either can affect the pass. Navy2 is another option, but being closest does not decide whether Navy3 is available.

questions.prompt: Place YOU where the puck has more room from Gold1 and both teammates stay ahead of YOU.
questions.explanation: Gold1 is closer to the puck than to YOU, so making room can come before choosing a target. From this example the puck sits about five metres from Gold1 instead of under two, and both navy teammates are still in front. Gold1 can follow, so look again before passing.

questions.prompt: If both teammates were covered, what could YOU do with the puck instead?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A useful reply names something YOU can do without a pass, such as carrying to a new angle, protecting the puck, or waiting for a teammate to move. Nothing in a still picture proves any of those would work.

scenarios.title: Handle the puck beside the boards
scenarios.objective: Notice pressure and nearby inside room while carrying.
scenarios.briefing: YOU control the puck beside the boards in the attacking end. Gold1 faces you from the goalward side. Navy2 offers an inside partner near the faceoff circle. This is a puck-control activity, not a checking drill. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU are close to the boards.
Gold1 is on the goalward side.
Navy2 is farther inside the rink.

questions.prompt: Which teammate is farther from the side boards?

options.text: Navy2
YOU
Neither player

questions.explanation: Navy2 stands well inside the rink. YOU are the one close to the side boards, about three metres from them.

questions.prompt: Which two things deserve a look before moving?

options.text: Gold1's pressure side
Navy2's location
A promise that every route works

questions.explanation: These are the source-supported cues; a safe route is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Explore a little inside space while keeping Navy2 available.
questions.explanation: The reference moves away from the boards and the goalward opponent. Other choices may work; no contact or travel-time result is certified.

questions.prompt: Arrange a careful control check.

options.text: Locate the nearby pressure
Notice inside room and support
Try a short controlled action

questions.explanation: This is one coaching routine, not a forced game answer.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 moves inside instead. Should you keep using the same inside spot?

options.text: Yes, the inside spot is always open
Recheck where Gold1 actually went before deciding
Turn back toward the boards without looking

questions.explanation: The useful space depends on where the pressure actually is. If Gold1 moves inside, that room can close and the board side can open, so the answer comes from looking rather than from a habit.

questions.prompt: How do the boards change the room you can use?
questions.explanation: They bound one side of the space. Discuss inside support or another available route without assuming a guaranteed escape.

questions.prompt: Gold1 stands between YOU and the net. Where does the open route to Navy2 run?

options.text: Away from Gold1, back toward the middle of the ice
Straight through Gold1 toward the net
Along the boards past Gold1

questions.explanation: Gold1 stands on the net side of the puck, and the line from the puck to Navy2 heads away from Gold1 toward the middle of the ice. Going along the boards past Gold1 skates into the pressure with the boards on your other side. Nothing here proves the pass or the route would be completed.

questions.prompt: What two things happen if YOU keep going toward the corner?

options.text: The boards curve in and the space gets tighter
Gold1 is already near that route
Navy2 becomes easier to reach

questions.explanation: The boards curve into the corner and Gold1 is nearby. Navy2 is back toward the middle, so continuing toward the corner can make that pass longer. A corner can still help YOU protect the puck; check the pressure and the lane.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 closer to give YOU a short, clear outlet.
questions.explanation: A shorter offer is easier to reach from a tight board-side spot, and this example keeps the line clear of Gold1, who stands on the net side of the puck. Navy2 could also stay wider to stretch the play; that depends on how hard Gold1 presses.

questions.prompt: What would YOU say out loud to Navy2 from this spot?
questions.explanation: YOU have the puck. You could tell Navy2 which side Gold1 is on, ask Navy2 to show a target, or say where YOU can send a pass. Useful talk helps your partner understand the next choice; it does not guarantee the play will work.

scenarios.title: Pressure before a wall reception
scenarios.objective: Read the pressure side before a planned pass reaches the wall.
scenarios.briefing: Navy2 holds the puck and plans a pass to YOU near the boards. Gold1 approaches from the circle side; Navy3 is a second navy option along the wall. This freeze is before the pass, so YOU cannot shoot or carry the puck yet. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The puck still belongs to Navy2.
Gold1 approaches from the circle side.

questions.prompt: Do YOU control the puck at this freeze?

options.text: Yes, YOU have it
No, Navy2 still has it
No, the puck is loose on the ice

questions.explanation: Navy2 is still the puck owner in this picture, so this is the moment before the planned reception. The puck is not loose.

questions.prompt: What can YOU notice before reception?

options.text: Pressure from Gold1
Navy3's supporting position
A guaranteed shooting chance

questions.explanation: Pressure and support are available information. A future shot is not established.

questions.prompt: Arrange this declared two-stage activity.

options.text: Read while Navy2 has the puck
Receive if the planned pass is made
Recheck before the next action

questions.explanation: The reception is conditional, and the next action depends on the new state.

questions.prompt: Show a slightly different receiving angle near the boards.
questions.explanation: The reference changes the approach angle. It is a suggestion, not proof the pass will arrive.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 comes along the boards instead. What is a useful response?

options.text: Reconsider the receiving angle
Use the old plan without looking
Shoot before receiving

questions.explanation: A different pressure side may call for a different touch or route.

questions.prompt: What can you do before the puck is yours?
questions.explanation: Look, communicate and prepare an available target. A puck action must wait for actual control.

questions.prompt: Imagine YOU receive the pass and Gold1 then covers the line back to Navy2. What can YOU do?

options.text: Carry to a new angle and check the pass to Navy2 again
Send it back on the covered line anyway
Stand still and wait for Navy2 to skate to YOU

questions.explanation: Imagine YOU have received the puck. YOU are now the carrier. A controlled move can change your passing angle to Navy2, but check Gold1 again before sending it. Navy3 may also offer a clear pass, or YOU may need to protect the puck.

questions.prompt: Which two things does this picture actually show?

options.text: Navy2 has the puck
Gold1 is nearer the middle of the ice than YOU
The pass has already been made

questions.explanation: Navy2 is the puck owner, and Gold1 stands nearer the middle of the ice while YOU wait closer to the boards. The pass has not happened; this freeze is before it.

questions.prompt: Place YOU where Navy2 would have a new option away from Gold1, after a pass back.
questions.explanation: This asks YOU to imagine the pass and the return. From this example Navy2 has an offer of about five metres on the board side, and the line to it stays well away from Gold1, who is nearer the middle. Other clear spots can work, and if Gold1 follows YOU the picture changes again.

questions.prompt: If YOU pass the puck back to Navy2, why would YOU keep skating?
questions.explanation: A useful answer says a player who stops can be easier to cover, and that moving gives the carrier a new option. This picture is the moment before the first pass, so the return pass is something to imagine rather than something shown.
